result: Gpr156 mutant mice exhibit normal otolith organ zonal organization with unchanged striolar surface area and hair cell density in both utricle and saccule compared to controls.
evaluation: Claims C5, C21-C24, and C27 collectively demonstrate that loss of GPR156 does not affect macular patterning. The data in Figure 1B-C show quantitative measurements with appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U test) confirming no significant differences in striolar organization between mutants and controls.

result: Type I and Type II hair cell numbers are preserved across all zones (LES, striola, MES) in Gpr156 mutant otolith organs.
evaluation: Claims C6, C25-C27 are supported by immunolabeling data in Figure 1D-I using SPP1 and SOX2 markers with two-way ANOVA statistical analysis. The quantification shows no significant differences in hair cell type distribution between mutants and controls across all zones.

result: Mechano-electrical transduction properties are normal in lateral extrastriolar (LES) hair cells of Gpr156 mutant mice, with no differences in peak MET current, displacement sensitivity, operating range, or adaptation kinetics.
evaluation: Claims C7, C28-C31 are supported by comprehensive electrophysiological recordings in Figures 2-4. The data show ~70% of LES HCs responded to stimulation regardless of genotype, with no significant differences in Boltzmann parameters (Gmax, X1/2, dx), operating range (~800-900 nm), or adaptation rates between mutants and controls.

result: Voltage-gated K+ conductances characteristic of Type I and Type II hair cells are preserved in Gpr156 mutants.
evaluation: Claims C32-C33 are supported by voltage-clamp data in Figure 3 showing that the distinctive electrophysiological properties of Type I HCs (large gK,L at rest, low input resistance ~50 MΩ) and Type II HCs (smaller voltage-gated conductance, higher input resistance ~500 MΩ) are maintained in mutants.

result: Hair cells in striola and MES zones show no systematic differences in electrophysiological properties despite Gpr156 expression throughout the maculae.
evaluation: Claims C34-C35 acknowledge that while Gpr156 is transcribed in all HCs, no striking systematic differences were observed in striola and MES zones. However, the authors explicitly note low statistical power (Supplementary file 4), making it uncertain whether subtle effects exist.

result: In zebrafish lateral-line neuromasts, gpr156 mutants lack the functional asymmetry between hair cell populations, with all HCs showing mechanosensitive responses comparable to Emx2-negative (anterior-sensing) cells.
evaluation: Claims C8, C40-C42, C71, and C73 are supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 5. The data show that mechanosensitive GCaMP6s responses in gpr156 mutants are significantly larger than control A-to-P HCs (p=0.0043) and comparable to control P-to-A HCs, demonstrating loss of functional asymmetry.

result: Afferent receptive fields and orientation-selective innervation patterns are preserved in mouse Gpr156 mutant utricles despite loss of the line of polarity reversal.
evaluation: Claims C9, C44-C51 are supported by dye-filling experiments (Figure 6) and Advillin-Cre genetic labeling (Figure 7). The data show that dimorphic afferents maintain normal terminal arbor organization, respect zonal boundaries, and selectively innervate HCs based on orientation (not HC orientation per se) in mutants.

result: In zebrafish neuromasts, afferent fibers maintain high selectivity for Emx2-positive or Emx2-negative hair cells in gpr156 mutants, independent of hair cell orientation.
evaluation: Claims C10, C101-C104 are supported by single afferent fiber labeling in Figure 9. Quantification shows that afferents in gpr156 mutants contact similar numbers of HCs per neuromast (p=0.48) and maintain high selectivity (control: 85.06±4.32%, gpr156: 81.29±3.17%, p=0.48) based on Emx2 expression despite all HCs responding to anterior flow.

result: Synaptic pairing is normal in gpr156 mutant zebrafish neuromasts, with no increase in unpaired pre- or post-synapses, contrasting with emx2 mutants.
evaluation: Claims C105-C109 are supported by immunolabeling data in Figure 10. The data show complete synapses are unchanged across genotypes, while emx2 mutants show significantly more unpaired synapses (presynapses p=0.02, postsynapses p<0.0001) but gpr156 mutants do not (presynapses p=0.29, postsynapses p=0.12).

result: Afferent firing patterns and excitability are preserved in LES afferents of Gpr156 mutants.
evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by current-clamp recordings in Figure 8. Both control and mutant LES afferents showed similar current thresholds (~100 pA) and sustained firing patterns at 3×Ithresh (~95% of afferents), indicating normal ion channel expression and excitability.

result: Gpr156 mutant mice show no overt vestibular dysfunction in basic postural and balance tests.
evaluation: Claims C11, C77-C79 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 11 and supplements. Mutants showed normal performance on balance beam, tail hanging, air righting, and contact inhibition tests, with no circling or head tremor behaviors at rest.

result: Gpr156 mutant mice exhibit severe swimming deficits characterized by underwater tumbling and inability to maintain upright posture, requiring significantly earlier rescue than controls.
evaluation: Claims C12, C55-C57, and C87 are supported by swimming test data in Figure 11B showing significantly reduced time to rescue in mutants (17.4±2.7s) compared to controls (49.9±3.0s, p<0.0001). This represents a major otolith-dependent behavioral deficit.

result: Semicircular canal-driven vestibular reflexes (VOR in dark and light, OKR, VOR adaptation) are normal in Gpr156 mutants.
evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are supported by comprehensive VOR and OKR testing in Figure 12A-F and supplement. Both genotypes showed comparable gain and phase responses across frequencies, normal OKR confirming no visual deficits, and similar VOR motor learning capacity.

result: Gpr156 mutants show impaired otolith-mediated steady-state OVAR responses with significantly reduced bias, while transient canal-mediated responses remain normal.
evaluation: Claims C13, C63-C66 are supported by OVAR testing in Figure 12G-H. Transient responses were comparable between genotypes, but steady-state bias was significantly reduced in mutants (0.039±0.26) compared to controls (3.85±0.54, p=4.03E-5), demonstrating specific otolith dysfunction.

result: GPR156 acts downstream of EMX2 to relay hair cell orientation and transduction information but not afferent selectivity.
evaluation: Claims C14-C16 and C89 represent the main conclusion supported by the combined mouse and zebrafish data. Loss of GPR156 prevents HC orientation reversal (Figures 1-2), affects mechanosensitivity in zebrafish (Figure 5), but preserves afferent selectivity in both species (Figures 6-10).

result: Hair cell orientation is controlled independently from other zonally differentiated properties, and afferent segregation depends on EMX2 but not GPR156 or HC orientation per se.
evaluation: Claims C67, C90-C92, and C112 are supported by the demonstration that Advillin-positive neurons segregate with HC orientation in controls but maintain segregation in Gpr156 mutants despite loss of orientation reversal (Figure 7), indicating EMX2 uses different effectors for orientation versus afferent patterning.

result: Zebrafish Emx2 may act through Gpr156 to impact Tmc2a/2b mechanotransduction channel function.
evaluation: Claim C72 is speculative and based on inference from the functional data. While the loss of functional asymmetry in gpr156 mutants suggests GPR156 affects Tmc channel function, the mechanism is not directly tested and remains hypothetical.

result: Gpr156 mutants show more severe swimming deficits than Emx2 mutants, potentially because aberrant vestibular signals are more deleterious than absent signals.
evaluation: Claims C85-C88 and C94-C98 compare behavioral phenotypes across models but rely heavily on speculation. While the swimming differences are documented, the explanations for why Gpr156 mutants are more severely affected (properly relayed but aberrant signals vs. absent/dampened signals) are not directly tested.

result: The Gpr156 mutant model is well-suited to specifically interrogate how HC orientation reversal influences vestibular function because it lacks confounding afferent patterning defects.
evaluation: Claims C99-C100 and C113 represent a methodological conclusion supported by the comprehensive characterization showing that Gpr156 mutants have isolated defects in HC orientation without affecting afferent selectivity, HC numbers, or electrophysiological properties, making it a cleaner model than Emx2 mutants.
